newsitem.title: GERMANY: Jewish leader urges Bonn to pay Holocaust claims.
newsitem.headline: Jewish leader urges Bonn to pay Holocaust claims.

text.p: Germany should quickly make long overdue restitution payments to eastern European survivors of Nazi concentration camps before the elderly Holocaust victims die, the head of a Jewish lobby group said on Tuesday.

Israel Singer, secretary general of the World Jewish Congress and leader of a claims delegation to Bonn, said time was running out for a large number of eastern European victims who never received any compensation for their suffering.

"We are fighting the clock, the biological clock," Singer told Reuters in an interview before two days of negotiations with senior German government officials. "The average age of the Holocaust survivors is now over 80. This gives us very little time to resolve the issue. It's five minutes after 12."

Singer said Germany had treated victims of the Holocaust who ended up in western Europe after World War Two generously and honourably. He said the Jewish Claims Conference (JCC) would press Bonn to treat eastern European survivors the same way.

"We are here to deal with those cases that have not yet been dealt with," Singer said, adding he had received assurances of support from Chancellor Helmut Kohl. "We are very optimistic. We have great hopes that these talks will indeed serve to deal with those people who are ageing rapidly."

Singer said the delegation, made up of officials from the United States, Israel and eastern Europe, would discuss the issue with Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl on Wednesday. Other meetings are planned with Finance Ministry officials.

Herbert Schmuelling, a government spokesman, said Bonn was also eager to reach a quick settlement with the survivors. But the opposition Greens party said the government had been dragging its feet for too long.

"The Jewish victims living in eastern Europe have been completely excluded from the monthly pension of 500 marks ($273) that Jews in western states have received," said Volker Beck, a Greens party leader. "It is time this 'Iron Curtain' came down."

Germany has paid about 100 billion marks in compensation since World War Two for victims of Nazi crimes and injustice, but Holocaust victims in eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union were excluded from remuneration during the Cold War.
The claims conference and other Jewish groups are demanding that anything between 15,000 and 40,000 eastern European survivors should be made eligible for German pensions.
"We are talking about persons who suffered greatly 50 or 55 years ago," Singer said.

"People were in concentration camps for three or four years and have yet to receive one cent in compensation or restitution for their suffering. We are here to discuss people who have not received any restitution and those numbers are considerable."
The former communist East Germany refused to pay reparations to Hitler's victims.
After the collapse of Communism, lobby groups said that eastern European victims were paid only a fraction of amounts given to western victims.
They argue that even though Germany set funds aside for them, this only amounted to a maximum of 1,000 marks in one-off payments, while people living in Germany received about 500 marks a month.
Many victims' groups have been further angered by reports that Germany has been paying supplementary pensions worth billions of marks each year to Nazi war criminals.

"That is a scandal," said Michel Friedman, a leader of the Central Council of Jews in Germany. "It is incomprehensible that the criminals are now enjoying pensions paid for by the German government while the victims are being shut out."

Bonn says Germany had set aside 1.5 billion marks for Jewish Holocaust survivors in Poland, Russia, Ukraine and Belarus and argued that these hard currency payments went far in the poor economies of the former eastern bloc.
But campaigners complain that victims in some countries have received no payments at all. ($ = 1.834 German Marks)
